pharm: Protein-tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks the constitutively active BCR-ABL kinase of the Philadelphia chromosome, as well as c-Kit, PDGFR, and SCF receptor kinases, inhibiting proliferation and inducing apoptosis in malignant cells.
quick: 400 mg/day (chronic CML/GIST); 600 mg/day (advanced CML, Ph+ ALL); 800 mg/day (DFSP)
Take with a meal and a large glass of water
Can cause fetal harm; avoid pregnancy; use effective contraception
Do not breastfeed during and for 1 month after last dose
Mild/moderate impairment increases exposure 1.5-2x; use caution
Caution - hepatotoxicity risk; avoid grapefruit juice
CBC, LFTs, weight/edema, LVEF if cardiac risk, TSH, renal function
summary: Imatinib mesylate is an oral BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor indicated for Philadelphia chromosome-positive CML and ALL, GIST (treatment and adjuvant), and several rarer PDGFR/c-Kit-driven malignancies. It has no formal boxed warning but a rich set of warnings: fluid retention/edema, cytopenias, severe hepatotoxicity, hemorrhage and GI perforation, congestive heart failure/LV dysfunction, hypereosinophilic cardiac toxicity, tumor lysis syndrome, growth retardation in children, and embryo-fetal toxicity. It is a CYP3A4 substrate and inhibitor, requiring attention to drug interactions and dose modification in hepatic impairment.
indications: Newly diagnosed adult and pediatric patients with Ph+ chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase
Ph+ CML in blast crisis, accelerated phase, or chronic phase after failure of interferon-alpha therapy
Adult patients with relapsed or refractory Ph+ acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
Pediatric patients with newly diagnosed Ph+ ALL in combination with chemotherapy
Adult patients with MDS/MPD associated with PDGFR gene re-arrangements
Adult patients with aggressive systemic mastocytosis (ASM) without the D816V c-Kit mutation or with unknown mutation status
Adult patients with hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) and/or chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL)
Adult patients with unresectable, recurrent, and/or metastatic dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP)
Patients with Kit (CD117)-positive unresectable and/or metastatic malignant GIST
Adjuvant treatment of adult patients following resection of Kit (CD117)-positive GIST

dosage.t: With a meal and a large glass of water
dosage.n: May increase to 600 mg/day for inadequate response or progression

dosage.c: Ph+ CML accelerated phase or blast crisis (adult)
dosage.n: May increase to 800 mg/day (400 mg twice daily) absent severe toxicity
No experience under 1 year of age
Avoid if D816V c-Kit mutation present; titrate to 400 mg as needed
Use 400 mg tablets to reduce iron exposure
Increase only if clear progression and no severe toxicity
Three years of treatment recommended in defined population

admin: Take orally with a meal and a large glass of water to minimize GI irritation
Doses of 400 mg or 600 mg once daily; 800 mg/day given as 400 mg twice daily
For 800 mg/day and above, use 400 mg tablets to reduce iron exposure
For patients unable to swallow, disperse tablets in water or apple juice (~50 mL per 100 mg tablet, ~200 mL per 400 mg tablet) and take immediately after disintegration
Do not crush; avoid skin/mucous membrane contact with crushed tablets and wash thoroughly if contact occurs
Continue treatment as long as there is no disease progression or unacceptable toxicity
moa: Imatinib mesylate is a protein-tyrosine kinase inhibitor that potently inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase, the constitutively active abnormal kinase created by the Philadelphia chromosome in CML. By blocking BCR-ABL it inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis in Ph+ leukemic cells. Imatinib also inhibits the receptor tyrosine kinases for platelet-derived growth factor (PDGFR) and stem cell factor (c-Kit/SCF), inhibiting PDGF- and SCF-mediated cellular events; in GIST it induces apoptosis in cells expressing an activating c-Kit mutation.

relative: Pre-existing cardiac disease or risk factors for cardiac failure
Conditions with high eosinophil levels (HES/MDS-MPD/ASM) - risk of cardiogenic shock at initiation
monitor: Complete blood counts (weekly x1 month, biweekly x2nd month, then periodically)
Liver function before initiation and monthly or as clinically indicated
Body weight and signs of fluid retention/edema
LVEF in patients with cardiac disease or risk factors; echocardiogram and troponin in HES/MDS-MPD/ASM at initiation
TSH in thyroidectomy patients on levothyroxine; renal function; growth in children

preg: Imatinib can cause fetal harm based on human and animal data, with postmarketing reports of spontaneous abortion and congenital anomalies. Rat studies showed teratogenicity and increased congenital abnormalities at doses near the highest human dose (800 mg/day) on a BSA basis. Advise women to avoid pregnancy while taking imatinib and to use effective contraception; if used in pregnancy or pregnancy occurs, apprise the patient of the potential hazard to the fetus.
lact: Imatinib and its active metabolite are excreted into human milk (milk:plasma ratio ~0.5 for imatinib, ~0.9 for the active metabolite; a breastfed infant could receive up to ~10% of the maternal therapeutic dose). Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose.
renal: Mild and moderate renal impairment increase dose-normalized imatinib exposure approximately 1.5- to 2-fold; use caution and monitor. A decline in renal function may occur during therapy; evaluate renal function at baseline and during treatment, with attention to risk factors for renal dysfunction.
hepatic: Mild and moderate hepatic impairment do not meaningfully change exposure to imatinib or its metabolite. Severe hepatic impairment increases imatinib Cmax and AUC; reduce the dose to 300 mg/day. Severe hepatotoxicity, including fatalities, can occur; assess liver function before initiation and monthly or as clinically indicated, and monitor closely when combined with hepatotoxic chemotherapy (e.g., high-dose acetaminophen).

major: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort) - reduce imatinib exposure; consider alternatives
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir) - significantly increase imatinib exposure
Warfarin - use low-molecular-weight or standard heparin instead (CYP2C9/3A4 metabolism affected)
High-dose methotrexate (>500 mg/m2) - imatinib delays methotrexate clearance
moderate: CYP3A4 substrates with narrow therapeutic windows (triazolobenzodiazepines, dihydropyridine CCBs, certain statins) - increased levels
CYP2D6 substrates with narrow therapeutic windows - increased levels
Acetaminophen/other hepatotoxins - additive liver injury risk
interactions.food: Take with a meal and a large glass of water; avoid grapefruit juice (increases plasma imatinib).
interactions.alcohol: Use caution due to additive hepatotoxicity risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor TSH (hypothyroidism in thyroidectomy patients on levothyroxine); monitor CBC, LFTs, and renal function.

serious: Severe fluid retention (pleural effusion, ascites, pulmonary/cerebral edema)
Congestive heart failure / left ventricular dysfunction
rare: Cardiogenic shock/LV dysfunction at initiation in hypereosinophilic conditions

monitoring: Complete blood counts weekly for the first month, biweekly for the second month, then periodically
Liver function tests before initiation and monthly or as clinically indicated
Body weight regularly; investigate unexpected rapid weight gain (fluid retention)
LVEF in patients with cardiac disease or risk factors; cardiac assessment (echo, troponin) at initiation in HES/MDS-MPD/ASM
TSH in thyroidectomy patients on levothyroxine
Renal function at baseline and during therapy
counsel: Always take with food and a large glass of water
Report sudden weight gain, swelling, or shortness of breath (fluid retention/heart failure)
Report fever, bruising, bleeding, black or bloody stools, or severe abdominal pain promptly
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or severe blistering rash
Avoid grapefruit juice; tell your clinician about all medicines, including warfarin and acetaminophen
Use effective contraception and do not breastfeed; this drug can harm an unborn or breastfed child
Caution with driving or operating machinery; report any growth concerns in children
pk: Supports once-daily dosing; 1.5-2.5x accumulation at steady state
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from moisture; dispense in a tight container
pearls: No formal boxed warning, but rich warnings: edema/fluid retention, cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, hemorrhage/GI perforation, CHF/LV dysfunction, and embryo-fetal toxicity
Always administer with food and a large glass of water to reduce GI irritation
Use heparin, not warfarin, for anticoagulation due to CYP interaction
Avoid grapefruit juice and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers
Confirm relevant molecular markers (PDGFR rearrangement, D816V c-Kit, FIP1L1-PDGFRalpha) before treating rarer indications
Cardiogenic shock/LV dysfunction can occur at initiation in hypereosinophilic conditions - obtain baseline cardiac assessment
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered with food, unless it is near the time of the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Experience with doses above 800 mg is limited and there is no specific antidote. Reported effects scale with dose: 1,200-1,600 mg - nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, edema, fatigue, muscle spasms, cytopenias, abdominal pain, headache; 1,800-3,200 mg - weakness, myalgia, increased CPK and bilirubin, GI pain; very high single doses (6,400 mg to 8-10 g) - vomiting, GI pain, neutropenia, transaminase elevation, facial swelling. Observe the patient and provide supportive care.
